nodes.label: Chapter 4 Network Layer Data Plane
nodes.rationale: Kurose and Ross, Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach, 9th edition (Pearson, 2025), slides on the network-layer data plane: service models, router internals, IP, NAT, IPv6, generalized forwarding, and middleboxes.

nodes.label: Data Plane
nodes.rationale: Local, per-router function that decides which output port an arriving datagram uses. Implemented in forwarding hardware and operates on a nanosecond timescale, separate from millisecond-scale control-plane software.

nodes.label: Control Plane
nodes.rationale: Network-wide logic that chooses the end-to-end path. Two approaches: traditional routing algorithms inside each router, or software-defined networking where a remote controller computes and installs forwarding tables. How tables are computed is deferred to the next chapter.

nodes.label: Forwarding
nodes.rationale: Move packets from a router's input link to the appropriate output link. Analogy: getting through a single interchange, as opposed to planning the whole trip (routing).

nodes.label: Routing
nodes.rationale: Determine the route packets take from source to destination using routing algorithms. Analogy: planning a trip, distinct from per-hop forwarding.

nodes.label: Internet Best-Effort Service
nodes.rationale: No guarantees of successful delivery, timing or order, or bandwidth. Simplicity enabled wide deployment; bandwidth provisioning, nearby replicated services (datacenters and CDNs), and congestion control of elastic traffic make performance good enough most of the time.

nodes.label: Intserv Guaranteed Service
nodes.rationale: Internet service model in RFC 1633 offering bandwidth, loss, order, and timing guarantees, contrasted with best effort.

nodes.label: Diffserv
nodes.rationale: Differentiated services (RFC 2475) with possible bandwidth, loss, and order guarantees. The IPv4 type-of-service field uses bits 0-5 for Diffserv and bits 6-7 for ECN.

nodes.label: ATM CBR and ABR
nodes.rationale: ATM Constant Bit Rate guarantees a constant rate, no loss, order, and timing. Available Bit Rate guarantees a minimum bandwidth and order but not timing.

nodes.label: Router Architecture
nodes.rationale: Input ports, high-speed switching fabric, output ports, and a routing processor. Forwarding is decentralized in port hardware; routing and management stay in the control-plane processor.

nodes.label: Longest Prefix Matching
nodes.rationale: Destination-based forwarding selects the forwarding-table entry whose address prefix is the longest match. Needed so a more-specific route can override an aggregated prefix. Often done in TCAM in one clock cycle regardless of table size; a Cisco Catalyst holds about 1M entries.

nodes.label: TCAM
nodes.rationale: Ternary content-addressable memory: present an address and retrieve the matching forwarding entry in one clock cycle independent of table size.

nodes.label: Switching Fabric
nodes.rationale: Transfers packets from input links to output links. Three types: via memory (CPU, two bus crossings, limited by memory bandwidth), via a shared bus (contention; 32 Gbps Cisco 5600 sufficient for access routers), and via an interconnection network (crossbar, Clos, multistage; cells switched in parallel). Cisco CRS uses 8 switching planes, each a 3-stage network, up to hundreds of Tbps. Desired rate is N times line rate.

nodes.label: Head-of-the-Line Blocking
nodes.rationale: If the fabric is slower than the combined input ports, input queues form. A datagram at the front blocked by output-port contention prevents later datagrams in that queue from moving, causing delay and loss on overflow.

nodes.label: Buffer Management
nodes.rationale: When output buffers fill because the fabric delivers faster than the link can send, a drop policy chooses victims: tail drop or priority drop. Marking (ECN, RED) signals congestion without necessarily dropping. Excess buffering, especially in home routers, increases delay and hurts real-time apps and delay-based congestion control.

nodes.label: RFC 3439 Buffering Rule
nodes.rationale: Rule of thumb: average buffering equal to a typical RTT (about 250 ms) times link capacity C. Example: a 10 Gbps link implies a 2.5 Gbit buffer. A later recommendation with N flows is RTT times C over square root of N.

nodes.label: Packet Scheduling
nodes.rationale: Decides which queued packet is sent next on a link. Policies: first-come-first-served, priority, round robin, and weighted fair queueing. Classification may use any header fields. These mechanisms, with buffer management, are how an ISP allocates resources.

nodes.label: FCFS Scheduling
nodes.rationale: First-come, first-served, also called FIFO: packets leave the output port in arrival order.

nodes.label: Priority Scheduling
nodes.rationale: Traffic is classified into priority classes. The scheduler always sends from the highest non-empty queue, with FCFS inside a class. Tied to who gets the best performance and to network-neutrality concerns about paid prioritization.

nodes.label: Round Robin Scheduling
nodes.rationale: The server cyclically scans class queues and sends one complete packet from each class that has a packet.

nodes.label: Weighted Fair Queuing
nodes.rationale: Generalized round robin. Class i with weight wi receives a weighted share wi over the sum of weights each cycle, giving a minimum bandwidth guarantee per traffic class.

nodes.label: Network Neutrality
nodes.rationale: How an ISP should share resources, technically via scheduling and buffer management, and socially via speech, innovation, and competition. The 2015 US FCC Open Internet order set three bright-line rules: no blocking, no throttling, and no paid prioritization, subject to reasonable network management. The order was rolled back in 2017 and that rollback was itself rolled back in 2024. Whether an ISP is a Title II telecommunications service (common-carrier duties) or a Title I information service under the Communications Acts of 1934 and 1996 determines how strongly it is regulated.

nodes.label: IP Protocol
nodes.rationale: Internet network-layer protocol present in every host and router. Defines datagram format, addressing, and packet-handling conventions. The sender encapsulates transport segments into datagrams; the receiver delivers segments up to the transport protocol.

nodes.label: IPv4 Datagram
nodes.rationale: Header includes version, header length, type of service (Diffserv and ECN), total length, identification, flags, fragment offset, TTL decremented at each router, upper-layer protocol, header checksum, 32-bit source and destination addresses, and optional options. Typical size is 1500 bytes or less; maximum is 64K. A 20-byte IP header plus 20-byte TCP header is 40 bytes before application data.

nodes.label: ICMP
nodes.rationale: Network-layer protocol for error reporting and router signaling, shown beside IP and the forwarding table.

nodes.label: IPv4 Addressing
nodes.rationale: A 32-bit identifier for each host or router interface, written in dotted-decimal notation. An interface connects a host or router to a physical link. Routers typically have many interfaces; hosts typically have one or two (Ethernet and 802.11). Vint Cerf is quoted on the choice of 32 bits. ICANN allocated the last IPv4 chunks to regional registries in 2011.

nodes.label: Subnet
nodes.rationale: Device interfaces that can reach each other without an intervening router. Detaching interfaces from hosts and routers leaves isolated islands, each a subnet. High-order bits are the subnet part; low-order bits are the host part. A /24 mask means the high-order 24 bits identify the subnet.

nodes.label: CIDR
nodes.rationale: Classless InterDomain Routing. The subnet portion has arbitrary length. Address format a.b.c.d/x, where x is the number of bits in the subnet portion (example 200.23.16.0/23).

nodes.label: DHCP
nodes.rationale: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol lets a host obtain an address when it joins, renew a lease, reuse addresses, and support mobile users (plug-and-play). Four messages: discover, offer, request, ack. Discover and offer may be skipped if the client reuses a previous address (RFC 2131). Also returns the first-hop router, DNS server name and address, and network mask. Often co-located in the router. DHCP is carried in UDP in IP in Ethernet and broadcast on the LAN (ports 68 and 67; Ethernet broadcast FFFFFFFFFFFF).

nodes.label: Route Aggregation
nodes.rationale: Hierarchical allocation lets an ISP advertise one prefix for many customer blocks (Fly-By-Night-ISP advertises 200.23.16.0/20 covering eight /23 organizations). When Organization 1 moves to ISPs-R-Us, that ISP advertises the more-specific 200.23.18.0/23, which is why longest-prefix match is required.

nodes.label: ICANN
nodes.rationale: Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (icann.org) allocates IP address blocks through five regional registries, which may allocate to local registries, and manages the DNS root zone including TLD delegation.

nodes.label: NAT
nodes.rationale: Network address translation lets every device in a local network share one public IPv4 address. The NAT router rewrites the source (IP, port) of outgoing datagrams, records the pair in a translation table, and rewrites the destination of incoming datagrams. Advantages: one ISP address, internal renumbering and ISP changes stay local, and inside hosts are not directly addressable. Controversial because routers process above layer 3, it was argued IPv6 should solve the shortage, it violates the end-to-end argument by manipulating port numbers, and NAT traversal is hard for inbound connections. Widely used in home, institutional, and 4G/5G networks.

nodes.label: Private IP Address Space
nodes.rationale: Prefixes 10/8, 172.16/12, and 192.168/16 are usable only inside the local network. The running example uses 10.0.0/24 inside and 138.76.29.7 as the single public NAT address.

nodes.label: IPv6
nodes.rationale: Motivated by IPv4 exhaustion, by faster forwarding with a 40-byte fixed header, and by per-flow treatment. 128-bit addresses, priority, flow label, payload length, next header, and hop limit. No checksum, no fragmentation or reassembly, and no options (options move to a next-header protocol). Google reported about 40 percent of clients using IPv6 in 2023; NIST reported one third of US government domains IPv6-capable. Deployment has taken more than 25 years.

nodes.label: IPv6 Tunneling
nodes.rationale: Transition without a flag day: an IPv6 datagram is carried as the payload of an IPv4 datagram between IPv4 routers (packet within a packet). Tunneling is also used extensively in 4G/5G. The outer IPv4 header uses the tunnel endpoints; the inner IPv6 header keeps the original source and destination.

nodes.label: Match Plus Action
nodes.rationale: Generalized forwarding matches bits in arriving headers and takes an action: drop, forward, modify, copy, log, or send to a controller. Many header fields can matter, unlike destination-IP-only forwarding. The same abstraction unifies a router (longest prefix, forward), a switch (destination MAC, forward or flood), a firewall (addresses and ports, permit or deny), and NAT (address and port, rewrite). It is a simple form of network programmability, with roots in active networking; P4 is the more general programming model today.

nodes.label: OpenFlow
nodes.rationale: Flow-table entries match link-layer fields (ingress port, source and destination MAC, Ethertype, VLAN id and priority), network-layer fields (IP ToS, protocol, source and destination), and transport ports. Actions: forward to ports, drop, modify headers, or encapsulate and send to the controller. Packet and byte counters are kept. Examples include destination-based forwarding, blocking TCP port 22, and blocking a specific source host.

nodes.label: Flow Table
nodes.rationale: A flow is defined by header field values across link, network, and transport layers. Each rule has a match pattern (wildcards allowed), an action, a priority to disambiguate overlapping patterns, and counters of bytes and packets. Orchestrated tables across switches produce network-wide behavior.

nodes.label: Software-Defined Networking
nodes.rationale: A remote controller, rather than a routing process in every router, computes forwarding tables and installs them. Control is logically centralized, often in a private or public cloud, while match-plus-action remains the local data-plane mechanism.

nodes.label: Middlebox
nodes.rationale: RFC 3234: any intermediary on the path that does more than the normal functions of an IP router. Examples: NAT (home, cellular, institutional), firewalls and IDS, load balancers, caches and CDNs, and application-specific boxes. Originally proprietary hardware; the trend is white-box hardware, open APIs, match-plus-action, and software differentiation. Described as the IP hourglass's middle-age love handles.

nodes.label: Network Functions Virtualization
nodes.rationale: Programmable network services running over white-box networking, computation, and storage, paired with SDN's centralized control and configuration.

nodes.label: Firewall
nodes.rationale: In the OpenFlow abstraction, a firewall matches IP addresses and TCP/UDP port numbers and permits or denies. Examples drop all datagrams to TCP port 22 and all datagrams from host 128.119.1.1. Deployed by enterprises, institutions, service providers, and ISPs, often with IDS.

nodes.label: P4
nodes.rationale: A more general form of per-packet network programming than match-plus-action, cited via p4.org, following the historical line of active networking.

nodes.label: IP Hourglass
nodes.rationale: The Internet's thin waist is a single network-layer protocol, IP, implemented by every connected device, with many protocols above (TCP, UDP, HTTP, SMTP, QUIC, DASH, RTP) and below (Ethernet, WiFi, Bluetooth, PPP, PDCP, copper, radio, fiber). Middleboxes operating inside the network are called the architecture's middle-age love handles.

nodes.label: RFC 1958 Architectural Principles
nodes.rationale: The goal is connectivity, the tool is the Internet Protocol, and the intelligence is end to end rather than hidden in the network. Three cornerstone beliefs: simple connectivity, IP as the narrow waist, and complexity at the edge.

nodes.label: End-to-End Argument
nodes.rationale: Saltzer, Reed, and Clark (1981): a function such as reliable transfer or congestion control can be completely and correctly implemented only with the knowledge of the application at the endpoints, so it cannot be provided solely as a feature of the communication system. An incomplete in-network version may still help performance. The slides contrast the 20th-century phone network (intelligence in switches), the pre-2005 Internet (intelligence at the edge), and the post-2005 Internet (programmable devices plus massive edge infrastructure).

nodes.label: OSPF and BGP
nodes.rationale: Path-selection algorithms implemented in routing protocols (OSPF, BGP) or, alternatively, in an SDN controller. They fill the forwarding table used by the data plane.

nodes.label: IP Fragmentation and Reassembly
nodes.rationale: A datagram larger than a link MTU is split inside the network and reassembled only at the destination. Identification, fragment offset, and flags order the pieces. Example: a 4000-byte datagram over a 1500-byte MTU becomes fragments of 1500, 1500, and 1040 bytes, with offsets in 8-byte units (0, 185, 370) because 1480/8 = 185.

nodes.label: MTU
nodes.rationale: Maximum transfer unit: the largest link-level frame a network link can carry. Different link types have different MTUs, which forces IP fragmentation of oversized datagrams.
